text: Mountains form when the rocky outer shell of the Earth gets pushed, pulled, cracked or melted. That shell is broken into huge plates that move a few centimetres a year. When they collide, rocks crumple upward into fold mountains. When they crack, blocks of land can lift or drop to make block mountains. When melted rock bursts through, it piles up into volcanic mountains.

There are also dome mountains, where rising rock bulges the surface without breaking through, and worn-down old ranges that are the stumps of ancient giants. Most big ranges are a mix of these. Every mountain is in a slow tug-of-war between forces lifting it and weather tearing it down.

st.reveal: The Aravallis are among the oldest mountain ranges on Earth, raised long before the dinosaurs. Rain, wind and rivers have been wearing them down ever since. The Himalaya are young and still rising, so they haven't had time to be rounded off.

sec.t:
The world's biggest ranges are fold mountains. They form when two plates push together and the rock layers between them buckle, like a rug shoved against a wall. The [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] began rising about 50 million years ago, when the Indian plate crashed into Asia. India is still pushing north at about 5 centimetres a year, and the range is still growing.

That is why climbers find [[fossil|fossils]] of sea creatures high in the Himalaya. The rocks were once mud on the floor of an ancient sea. Black stones containing [[@ammonites|ammonite]] fossils, called shaligram, are found along the Kali Gandaki river in Nepal, and many Hindus treat them as sacred. The Alps in Europe and the Appalachians in the USA are also fold mountains.

Volcanic mountains are built from melted rock, called [[magma|magma]], that rises through cracks and erupts as [[lava|lava]] and ash. Each eruption adds a new layer. [[@mount-fuji|Mount Fuji]] in Japan and Mount [[@kilimanjaro|Kilimanjaro]] in Tanzania are cone-shaped volcanoes built this way.

Some of the biggest volcanoes are under the sea. Mauna Kea in [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]] rises over 4,200 metres above sea level, but its base sits deep on the ocean floor. From bottom to top, it is over 10,000 metres tall. India's only active volcano, on Barren Island in the Andaman Sea, is also mostly underwater.

Sometimes magma pushes up from below but doesn't erupt. It cools underground, bulging the rock above it into a dome. Over time, [[erosion|erosion]] strips away the softer top layers and leaves the hard core standing as hills.

The Black Hills of South Dakota formed partly this way. Their hard [[granite|granite]] was later carved into the four presidents' faces of [[@mount-rushmore|Mount Rushmore]]. The Black Hills are also sacred to the Lakota people, who know them as Paha Sapa.

Mountains don't last forever. Rain, frost, [[@glaciers|glaciers]] and rivers wear them down. The Aravalli hills in Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi are among the oldest mountains on Earth. They were raised long before the dinosaurs and were probably once very tall. Now their highest point, Guru Shikhar at Mount Abu, is about 1,722 metres.

The [[@appalachians|Appalachians]] tell a similar story. Hundreds of millions of years ago they may have rivalled the Himalaya. Today their rounded, forested ridges are gentle enough for long family hikes. The Appalachian Trail runs along them for about 3,500 kilometres, from Georgia to Maine.

text: If every [[glacier|glacier]] and ice sheet on Earth melted, the sea would rise by about 65 to 70 metres. That's higher than a 20-storey building. Huge stretches of coastline would vanish, including most of Bangladesh, the Netherlands and Florida, and cities from Mumbai to New York.

It wouldn't happen overnight. Scientists think melting all the ice would take thousands of years, even with fast warming. But some of it is already melting, and the sea has risen about 10 cm since 1993.

st.prompt: If all the floating sea ice in the Arctic melted, how much would sea level rise?

options.t: Almost not at all
About 7 metres
About 70 metres

st.reveal: Floating ice already displaces its own weight in water, just like an ice cube in a glass. When it melts, the level hardly changes. The big rise comes from ice sitting on land, in Antarctica and Greenland.

myth: The melting of Arctic sea ice is what makes the sea rise.
Arctic sea ice is already floating, so melting it adds almost nothing. Rising seas come mainly from land ice melting into the ocean, and from seawater expanding as it warms.

sec.t:
Almost all of Earth's ice sits on land in two places. [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] holds about nine-tenths of it, in a sheet up to about 4.8 km thick. That alone could raise the seas by about 58 metres.

Greenland holds most of the rest, enough for about 7 metres. Mountain [[@glaciers|glaciers]], like those in the Himalaya, the Alps and Alaska, add less than half a metre between them. But they matter in other ways, because hundreds of millions of people in India and nearby countries depend on rivers fed by Himalayan snow and ice.

When ice floats, it pushes aside its own weight of water. So when floating ice melts, the water level barely changes. That's why melting Arctic sea ice adds almost nothing to sea level. You can test this with an ice cube in a full glass.

Ice on land is different. When it melts and runs into the ocean, it adds new water. That is why scientists watch Greenland and Antarctica so closely. And as seawater warms, it expands a little, which also raises the sea.

sec.h: How fast is the sea rising now?
sec.t:
NASA measures sea level using satellites. In 2024, it rose by about 0.59 cm, faster than scientists had expected. The rate has more than doubled since 1993.

That doesn't sound like much, but a few centimetres can make storm floods reach much further inland. In the Sundarbans, where India and Bangladesh share the world's largest mangrove forest, some islands have already been swallowed by the sea and many families have had to move.

Ice is heavy. The Antarctic ice sheet presses the rock beneath it down into the Earth by hundreds of metres. When ice melts, the land slowly bounces back up.

This is happening today in places like Scandinavia and Canada, which were covered by thick ice in the last ice age. Parts of them are still rising by about 1 cm a year, more than 10,000 years after the ice left.

Sea levels have gone up and down many times. About 20,000 years ago, during the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]], so much water was locked in ice that the sea was about 120 metres lower than today. People could walk from Asia to North America, and from England to France.

About 3 million years ago, when Earth was a little warmer than today, the seas were probably more than 10 metres higher. That's why scientists say the choices people make about warming the planet now will shape the coastlines of the far future. Meanwhile, the water is already creeping up a few millimetres every year, and [[@sea-level-rise|rising seas]] are changing coasts right now.

text: The moon with hundreds of volcanoes is Io, one of the four big moons of Jupiter. It has about 400 active volcanoes, more than any other world we know, including Earth. Some of them spray plumes of gas and dust hundreds of kilometres above the surface.

Io is about the size of our own Moon. But instead of grey dust and [[crater|craters]], it is covered in yellow, orange, red and black patches of sulphur and fresh [[lava|lava]]. Photos of it are often compared to a pizza.
Io stays hot because Jupiter's [[gravity|gravity]] keeps squeezing it, heating its rock from inside.

st.prompt: What keeps Io's insides hot enough for so many volcanoes?

options.t: Squeezing by Jupiter's gravity as Io orbits
Heat from the Sun
Leftover heat from a giant meteorite crash

st.reveal: Io's orbit is slightly stretched, so Jupiter's pull on it keeps changing. The moon is squeezed and stretched over and over, and that friction heats its rock. Scientists call this tidal heating.

d.try: Take a soft rubber ball or a lump of modelling clay and squeeze it hard in your hand again and again for a minute. Notice that it gets slightly warm. Io is heated in a similar way, by being squashed and stretched by Jupiter's gravity.
myth: Moons are dead, cold rocks where nothing ever happens.
Io is the most volcanically active place known in the Solar System. Other moons have geysers, ice volcanoes and hidden oceans, so moons can be some of the busiest worlds around.
facts: about 3,640 km across, slightly bigger than our Moon

sec.t:
[[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] is more than 300 times as heavy as Earth. Io [[orbit|orbits]] close to it, going round once every 42 hours. Its path is not a perfect circle, so sometimes Io is a little closer to Jupiter and sometimes a little further away.

That means Jupiter's pull on Io keeps changing. The moon's solid surface bulges up and down, by as much as 100 metres, as it goes around. That is taller than a 30-storey building, rising and falling every day and a half.

On Earth, the Moon's pull raises the ocean [[@tides|tides]]. On Io there are no oceans, so the rock itself is pulled. All that bending creates heat, the same way a paper clip warms up when you bend it back and forth. The other big moons, Europa and Ganymede, keep tugging on Io's orbit, so the squeezing never stops.

Galileo Galilei discovered Io in January 1610 with one of the first telescopes. For more than 350 years it was just a dot of light. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] named it after Io, a character from Greek myths, but knew almost nothing about its surface.

In March 1979, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft flew past. A few days later, a [[navigation|navigation]] engineer named Linda Morabito was studying an image to help work out the craft's position. She noticed a strange curved cloud rising from the edge of Io. It was a volcanic plume, the first active volcano ever seen beyond Earth.

Just days before, three scientists had published a paper predicting that tidal heating might make Io volcanic. They were right.

{{story:galileo}}

Io's biggest volcano is Loki Patera, a lava lake about 200 km across. That is wider than the distance from Mumbai to Pune. Its surface cools and sinks, then fresh lava wells up, in waves that sweep across the lake.

NASA's Juno spacecraft flew close to Io in December 2023 and February 2024. Its pictures showed islands in Loki Patera, and a surface so smooth that Juno saw sunlight glinting off it like glass.

Some of Io's lava seems hotter than almost any that erupts on Earth today. The famous volcano Pele has thrown up plumes about 300 km high, with material raining back down in a red ring more than 1,000 km wide.

Io loses about a tonne of material to space every second. Sulphur and oxygen from its volcanoes are swept away by Jupiter's huge magnetic field, forming a glowing doughnut of charged gas around the planet.

That doughnut, and the [[radiation|radiation]] around Jupiter, make Io a deadly place for spacecraft. Probes have to zoom in and out quickly to protect their electronics.

Io is the most extreme of Jupiter's moons, but not the only strange one. Its neighbour is icy where Io is hot, and the same squeezing may keep a hidden ocean liquid under its shell. And the strangest part? That neighbour, [[@europa|Europa]], might be one of the best places to search for life beyond Earth.

text: Aluminium is everywhere because it is light, it doesn't rust away, it carries electricity well and it is easy to shape. It weighs about a third as much as [[@steel|steel]] for the same size. You'll find it in drink cans, foil, window frames, bicycles, pressure cookers, phones, power lines and aeroplanes.

It is also the most common metal in the Earth's crust, about 8% by weight. The catch is that it never sits around as pure metal. It is locked in rock, mostly an ore called bauxite, and getting it out takes a lot of electricity.

st.prompt: Aluminium is the most common metal in the ground. Why was it once more expensive than silver?

options.t: It is locked tightly inside rocks and was very hard to separate
It was only found at the bottom of the sea
Kings had banned people from digging it up

st.reveal: Aluminium clings very strongly to oxygen in rocks. Before 1886, freeing it took costly chemicals and gave only tiny amounts. Using electricity made it cheap almost overnight.

Both sides work the same. Foil is so thin that, in the last stage of rolling, two sheets go through the rollers together. The sides touching the polished rollers come out shiny and the sides touching each other come out dull.

sec.t:
Aluminium was first made as a metal in the 1820s, using expensive chemicals. For decades, it came out in tiny lumps. Emperor Napoleon III of France is said to have served his most honoured guests with aluminium cutlery while lesser guests used gold. The story may be partly legend, but aluminium really was a luxury.

The Washington Monument in the US capital was finished in 1884. Builders topped it with a small aluminium pyramid, about 23 centimetres tall. It was one of the largest single pieces of the metal ever cast at that time, and it was put on show in a New York jewellery shop before going up.

sec.h: From red earth to soft drink can
sec.t:
Bauxite is a reddish, crumbly rock that forms in hot, rainy places when other minerals wash out of the soil. India has large deposits, especially in the hills of [[@odisha|Odisha]], where the company NALCO runs mines and refineries. Australia, Guinea and Brazil are other big sources.

First, bauxite is crushed and cooked with chemicals to make alumina, a white powder like flour. About two tonnes of alumina make one tonne of aluminium. The smelting step uses so much power that aluminium plants are often built near big power stations or dams. In 2024, China made more than half of the world's aluminium, and India was in second place.

Iron [[@rust|rusts]], flaking and crumbling until it is gone. Aluminium reacts with air even faster, but in a useful way. In a split second, it grows a skin of aluminium oxide only a few millionths of a millimetre thick. This tough, see-through layer seals the metal underneath and stops it reacting any further.

That's why an aluminium ladder can sit in the rain for years and still look fine. It's also why aluminium is used in planes and ships, where weight and corrosion both matter.

Aluminium can be melted and reused again and again without getting worse. Recycling it uses only about 5% of the energy needed to make new metal from bauxite. A large share of all the aluminium ever made is still in use today, in buildings, cars and cables.

In India, kabadiwalas, the people who buy old newspapers and scrap, have long paid for old aluminium pots and cans. Melted down and rolled out again, an old can may be back on a shop shelf within a few months, holding a cold drink.

text: An electric car has no petrol tank and no engine full of [[piston|pistons]]. Instead, it has a big battery, usually a flat pack stretched under the floor, and one or more electric motors.

When you press the accelerator, [[@electricity-made|electricity]] flows from the battery to a box of electronics. That box controls how much power the motor gets. Inside the motor, the electricity creates magnetic forces that push a central shaft round and round. Gears pass that spin to the wheels. There is no burning, no exhaust and hardly any noise.
To refill, you plug the car into [[@chargers|a charger]], at home or at a charging station. Electricity flows back into the [[@batteries|battery]], ready for the next trip.

st.prompt: When an electric car brakes gently, where does much of its moving energy go?

options.t: Back into the battery
Out of the exhaust pipe
Into the brake pads as sparks

st.reveal: The motor switches roles and becomes a generator. The car's movement spins it, making electricity that flows back into the battery and slows the car down. This is called regenerative braking. Normal brakes still do the job when a sudden stop is needed.

They have no exhaust, so they keep city air cleaner. But making their batteries takes energy and mining, and the electricity that charges them may come from coal. Most studies find that over its whole life an electric car usually produces less carbon dioxide than a petrol car, and the gap grows as power stations get cleaner.

sec.t:
Electric motors are very simple compared with petrol engines. A petrol engine has hundreds of moving parts, from pistons and valves to the gearbox. An electric motor has one main spinning part. That means less to wear out and fewer oil changes.

Motors are also very efficient. Roughly 85–90% of the battery's energy ends up moving the car. A petrol car turns only about a quarter of its fuel's energy into motion. The rest is lost as heat.

Electric motors also give their full pushing force from the moment they start turning. That's why many electric cars shoot forward so quickly when the light turns green.

Electric cars were popular more than a century ago. Around 1900, according to the US Department of Energy, about a third of the cars on American roads ran on batteries. They were quiet, clean and easy to start, unlike petrol cars, which had to be cranked by hand.

Then, in 1908, Henry Ford launched the cheap petrol-powered [[@made-cars|Model T]]. Texas oil made petrol cheap, and by 1912 an electric starter removed the need for hand cranking. Electric cars faded away. They came back in the 2000s and 2010s, once lithium-ion batteries, the kind in phones and laptops, became powerful and cheap enough.

In India, the electric revolution has started with smaller vehicles. Battery e-rickshaws now carry passengers in towns across the country, and electric scooters are sold by the lakh. Delhi, Bengaluru and other cities run electric buses.

How clean an electric car really is depends on where its electricity comes from. In places where most power comes from coal, the benefit is smaller. As countries build more [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] and [[@wind-turbines|wind farms]], electric cars get cleaner too. Making the batteries needs metals like lithium, nickel and cobalt, so engineers are working on ways to [[@batteries-recycle|recycle old batteries]] and on new kinds that need fewer rare materials. That could matter a lot in the fight against [[@climate-change|climate change]].

text: Lift the lid of a flatbed scanner and you'll see a sheet of glass. Under it sits a long, thin bar carrying a lamp and a row of tiny light [[sensor|sensors]]. When you press scan, a small motor pulls the bar slowly from one end of the page to the other.

As it moves, the lamp lights a narrow strip of the page. Light bounces off the paper. White paper reflects a lot of light, and dark ink reflects very little. The sensors measure how bright each tiny spot is and turn that into a number.
Each strip becomes one row of [[@pixels|pixels]]. Thousands of rows, stacked top to bottom, make the finished image.

st.prompt: Why does a scanner need its own bright light inside?

options.t: To shine on the page so the sensor can measure the reflected light
To warm the paper so the ink shows up
To dry the ink before it smudges

st.reveal: The sensor measures how much light bounces back from each tiny spot. White paper reflects a lot, black ink very little. The scanner's own lamp makes sure every page is lit the same way.

d.try: Take a piece of squared graph paper and a simple black-and-white drawing. Lay the graph paper over it and fill in every square that is more than half black. You've just "scanned" the picture at low resolution. Try again with smaller squares and see how much sharper it gets.
myth: A scanner takes a photo of the whole page at once, like a camera.
A flatbed scanner uses a narrow strip of sensors that slides down the page, reading one thin line at a time. The computer stitches thousands of lines together into one picture.

sec.t:
Scanners are measured in dots per inch, or dpi. At 300 dpi, a common setting for documents, every inch of the page is split into 300 dots across and 300 down. That's 90,000 dots for each square inch, or about 14,000 for a square centimetre.

More dots give sharper detail and much bigger files. Museums and libraries scanning old maps or [[manuscript|manuscripts]] may use 600 dpi or more, so researchers can zoom in on faded ink. A photo scanned at 1,200 dpi can be printed many times bigger than the original without looking blurry. That's how old family photos get turned into posters.

For colour, the scanner measures each dot three times, through red, green and blue filters, or by flashing red, green and blue lights in turn. Mixing the three values gives the dot's true colour.

In 1957, the American engineer Russell Kirsch and his team at the National Bureau of Standards built a drum scanner for one of the country's first computers. The first image they fed in was a photo of Kirsch's baby son, Walden.

The scan was 176 dots wide and 176 high, just 30,976 dots in total, each one either black or white. It was rough and blocky, but it was the first time a photograph had been turned into numbers inside a computer. Almost every digital photo since has worked on the same idea.

A scan of a letter is just a picture. A computer can't search it or edit it until software reads the shapes of the letters and turns them into text. This is called optical character recognition, or OCR.

In 1976, the American inventor Ray Kurzweil showed a reading machine that scanned printed books and read them aloud with a computer voice. It was built for [[@blindness-tech|blind readers]], and was one of the first machines to recognise many different fonts. Today, OCR runs quietly in phone apps and in national libraries digitising millions of old books.

Shops use a different kind of scanner, a laser that sweeps across a [[@barcodes|barcode]] and measures the gaps between its stripes. A [[@photocopiers|photocopier]] is really a scanner and a printer in one box. And your phone camera can now flatten, straighten and sharpen a photo of a page so well that many people never touch a flatbed at all.

text: Germs often stick to your hands in oily, greasy dirt, and water alone slides right off grease. Soap fixes this. Each soap [[molecule|molecule]] has a head that loves water and a tail that loves oil.
The oily tails dig into the grease, and the water-loving heads face outward. The grease gets wrapped up in tiny balls that rinse away, taking germs with them.
Soap doesn't need to kill a germ to get rid of it. Most of the work is lifting germs off your [[@skin|skin]] so the water can wash them down the drain.

st.prompt: Why doesn't water alone wash away greasy dirt very well?

options.t: Water and oil don't mix
Water is too cold
Grease is invisible

st.reveal: Water slides right off oil. Soap molecules grab the grease with one end and the water with the other, so the grease gets carried away.

d.try: Rub a few drops of cooking oil over your hands, then sprinkle on a pinch of cinnamon powder to stand in for germs. Rinse with water alone and see how much stays stuck. Then wash with soap for 20 seconds, scrubbing between your fingers and around your nails, and compare.
myth: Antibacterial soap is much better than ordinary soap for washing your hands at home.

For everyday handwashing, ordinary soap and water work just as well. In 2016, the US Food and Drug Administration found no proof that antibacterial chemicals in home soaps worked better, and banned several of them.

sec.t:
Some viruses have an outer coat made of fatty material. Soap tails can wedge into that coat and break it apart, which destroys the virus. The flu virus and the virus that causes COVID-19 both have this kind of coat, which is why [[@body-handwashing-history|handwashing]] was such important advice during the [[pandemic|pandemic]].

Many [[bacteria|bacteria]] are tougher, but soap and scrubbing still loosen them from the skin and wash them away.

In 1847, a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed something terrible at a [[@hospitals|hospital]] in Vienna. Many more mothers died after giving birth on the ward run by doctors than on the ward run by midwives. The doctors often came straight from examining dead bodies.

Semmelweis made them wash their hands in a chlorine solution, and deaths on that ward fell sharply. Many doctors laughed at him. Germs hadn't been discovered yet, and the idea that their own hands spread disease offended them. Today, washing hands with soap is one of the cheapest and best ways to stop many illnesses from spreading.

People have made soap-like cleaners for thousands of years, often by boiling fats or oils with ashes.

In India, families long washed hair and clothes with reetha, the soapnut, whose dried fruit makes a lather in water, and with shikakai pods. They work for a similar reason: they contain natural chemicals that behave a lot like soap.

Not every germ is an enemy. Your skin and gut are home to trillions of friendly [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]] that help digest food and crowd out harmful ones. Washing your hands removes some of them for a while, but they quickly grow back.

Washing matters most at certain moments: before eating or cooking, after using the toilet, after blowing your nose, and after playing outside or with animals. The germs that do get past your skin then meet your [[@immune-system|immune system]], the body's own defence force.

Global Handwashing Day is held every year on 15 October. Schools in India, the USA and many other countries use it to teach good handwashing. A bar of soap costs very little, yet health experts count it among the most useful tools in medicine.

text: A phone does two jobs, one at each end. When you speak, [[@voice|your voice]] makes the air shake. Inside the phone, a microphone has a thin part that shakes along with it. Those shakes are turned into a changing electrical signal, a pattern that matches your voice.

That signal travels to the other phone, along wires or as radio waves. There, a tiny loudspeaker does the reverse. It uses the signal to shake a thin sheet back and forth, which shakes the air, which reaches your friend's ear as your voice. The whole trip can cross continents in a fraction of a second.

st.prompt: When you talk on a mobile phone, how does your voice get from your phone to the nearest tower?

options.t: As radio waves
As sound waves through the air
Through wires hidden underground

st.reveal: Your phone turns your voice into a stream of numbers and sends them as radio waves to a tower, which may be a kilometre or more away. From there, the call usually travels through cables and other towers to the person you are calling.

d.try: Make a string telephone. Poke a small hole in the bottom of two paper cups with a pencil, thread a long piece of string through, and tie a knot inside each cup. Pull the string tight and take turns talking and listening. Your voice shakes the cup, the cup shakes the string, and the string shakes the other cup.
myth: When you talk on the phone, your actual voice travels down the wire.

Sound can't travel far along a wire. The phone turns your voice into an electrical or radio copy, which zips along almost at the speed of light. The phone at the other end turns that copy back into sound.
facts: close to the speed of light

sec.t:
[[@sound-travel|Sound]] is just air being pushed and pulled very quickly. A deep voice shakes the air slowly, a squeaky one shakes it fast. A microphone has a light sheet, called a [[diaphragm|diaphragm]], that moves with these pushes. In many [[@microphones|microphones]], the moving diaphragm is attached to a coil of wire near a [[@magnets-how|magnet]], and moving wire near a magnet makes a small electric current.

The current rises and falls in exactly the same pattern as your voice. The loudspeaker at the other end works the same way backwards: current flows through a coil, the magnet pushes it, and the coil shakes a paper or plastic cone.

On 10 March 1876, in Boston, Alexander Graham Bell spoke into his new device and his assistant Thomas Watson heard him in another room. Bell had received his patent a few days earlier. He was not alone, though. Elisha Gray in the USA and Antonio Meucci, an Italian living in New York, had been working on similar ideas. Arguments over who came first went on for years, and some still go on. You can follow that story in [[@telephone-history|the history of the telephone]]. Bell himself kept experimenting all his life, with flying machines, hydrofoil boats and even a way to send sound on a beam of light.

{{story:telegraph}}

Early phones were joined by wires to an exchange, where operators plugged cables into a board to connect one caller to another. Within a few years, exchanges were opening around the world, including in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in the 1880s. Later, machines did the connecting automatically. Landline calls still travelled along copper wires for most of the twentieth century. Today many go as flashes of light through thin glass threads called optical fibres, which can carry thousands of calls at once.

A mobile phone has no wire at all. It turns your voice into numbers, a stream of 0s and 1s, and sends them as [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] to the nearest tower. The tower passes them into a network of cables, some lying on the ocean floor, and eventually to another tower near your friend.

On 3 April 1973, a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper stood on a street in New York and made the first call from a handheld mobile phone. It weighed about a kilogram, roughly as much as a bag of sugar, and its battery lasted around half an hour of talking. Charging it took about ten hours.

In India, the first mobile call came on 31 July 1995, when the Chief Minister of West Bengal, Jyoti Basu, called the Union Telecom Minister, Sukh Ram, from Kolkata to Delhi. Calls were expensive then. Today India has more than a billion mobile connections, carried by [[@mobile-networks|mobile networks]] that reach high into the Himalaya.

text: India's nomadic communities are groups who move from place to place for their living, instead of staying in one village. Some are herders who follow fresh grass with their animals. Others were traders, performers, healers or craftspeople who travelled from village to village selling their skills.

There are hundreds of such communities, from the Gaddi shepherds of Himachal to the Rabari camel herders of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Many have now settled down, at least for part of the year. Together with groups once called "criminal tribes", they may number around 10 to 12 crore people, though nobody has ever properly counted.

st.prompt: Why do herders like the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh move their flocks every year?

options.t: To follow fresh grass as the seasons change
Because the government tells them to
To avoid paying rent

st.reveal: In summer, high mountain meadows turn green while the lowlands dry out. In winter, snow buries the meadows. So herders walk up in spring and down in autumn, following the grass their animals need.

n.certNote: Nobody knows exactly how many nomadic and formerly nomadic people live in India. A 2008 government commission estimated 10 to 12 crore for the wider group, but India has never fully counted them.

d.try: Pretend your family must move every few months. Pack everything you think you would need for one week into a single school bag. Then list what you had to leave behind, and talk about which things you would miss most.
myth: Nomads wander about with no plan.
Most herding communities follow the same routes, at the same times of year, that their families have used for generations. They know exactly which meadow will be green and which well will have water.

sec.t:
Herding nomads move with the seasons. Each spring, Gaddi shepherds lead their sheep and goats up into the high meadows of the Himalaya. In autumn, before the snow, they walk back down to the warm valleys. The trek can take weeks and cross passes higher than 4,000 metres.

Bakarwals in Jammu and Kashmir do the same with goats and sheep. Van Gujjars in Uttarakhand move herds of buffaloes between forests and hills. High in Ladakh, Changpa families live in yak-hair tents and herd goats whose soft undercoat becomes [[@art-pashmina|pashmina]] wool. The goats grow that fleece to survive winters that drop well below minus 20 °C.

Not every nomad herded animals. For centuries, Banjara traders drove long lines of bullocks loaded with salt and grain across India. Some [[caravan|caravans]] had thousands of animals, and armies hired them to carry supplies. Their women still wear some of India's most dazzling clothes, stitched with tiny mirrors, cowrie shells and old coins that flash and jingle as they walk.

Today Banjara and Lambadi families live mostly in settled hamlets called *tandas*, from Rajasthan to Telangana and Karnataka. Many still speak their own language, Gor Boli, which has no script of its own but is passed on through songs.

Nat families were acrobats and tightrope walkers. Bahurupis were mimics and actors who dressed up as gods, kings or police officers. In Rajasthan, the Kalbelia were snake charmers. Their swirling black-skirted dance is now on UNESCO's list of the world's living heritage, and some Kalbelia dancers have performed on stages around the world.

{{story:people-shepherds-himalaya}}

sec.h: A law that branded whole communities
sec.t:
In 1871 the British passed the Criminal Tribes Act. It labelled entire communities, often wandering ones, as "born criminals". Every adult had to report to the police, and children grew up under suspicion. It was a deeply unfair law that judged people by their birth.

India repealed it in 1949, and in 1952 the communities were "denotified", or removed from that list. Many still mark 31 August as their freedom day. But prejudice lasted much longer than the law, and some of these families still struggle to get land, school places or ID papers.

Modern life has squeezed the old routes. Grazing land has become farms, roads and towns. Forests have fences. Camels and bullocks are no longer needed to carry goods. Many children of herders now go to school and take city jobs, while grandparents keep the flocks.

Some government schemes now run seasonal hostels, so herders' children can study while families move. India's 2027 [[census|census]] may count denotified tribes separately for the first time since 1911, which would finally show how many people belong to these groups. Herders still bring animals to great fairs like [[@india-wonder-pushkar|Pushkar]], and their wandering songs fed much of India's [[@folk-music-india|folk music]]. And the long walks themselves? Shepherds are not the only ones. Wildebeest, caribou and elephants make journeys every year that rival any herder's, as the story of [[@animal-migration-land|animal migration]] shows.

text: The Right to Information, or RTI, is a law that lets citizens ask the government questions and get answers on paper. In India, anyone can write to a public office and ask for records: how much a road cost, why a ration card was refused, how many doctors a hospital has. The office must reply within 30 days.

The idea is simple. Governments spend the people's money, so the people should be able to see how. Information that used to sit in locked files can now be asked for by a farmer, a student or a retired teacher, without hiring anyone.

st.prompt: How long does a government office in India usually have to answer an RTI request?

6 months

st.reveal: The law gives public offices 30 days to reply. If the question concerns someone's life or liberty, they must answer within 48 hours. An official who delays without good reason can be fined.

d.try: With an adult, think of one question you'd like a public body to answer, such as how much was spent repairing your nearest park or how many teachers your local government school has. Write it out clearly in one or two sentences, the way an RTI request would be. You don't have to send it; notice how a precise question is easier to answer.
myth: Only lawyers or journalists can file an RTI request.
Any Indian citizen can file one, on paper or online, without giving a reason for asking. People below the poverty line don't have to pay the fee.

sec.t:
You write a short letter or fill in a form online, addressed to the office's Public Information Officer, and pay a small fee, usually ₹10 for central government offices. You don't need to say why you want the information. The officer must answer within 30 days, or within 48 hours if a person's life or liberty is at risk.

If the reply is late or unhelpful, you can appeal to a senior officer and then to an Information Commission, which can fine officials who delay without reason. There is a Central Information Commission in Delhi for national offices, and each state has its own commission for state offices. Some records are protected, such as matters of national security, cabinet papers before a decision is made, and personal details that would invade someone's [[@privacy|privacy]].

Sweden passed one of the first freedom-of-information laws in 1766, as part of a law on press freedom. The United States passed its Freedom of Information Act in 1966, and President Lyndon Johnson signed it on 4 July, Independence Day. Reporters use it to uncover stories, and historians use it to open old government files. Today well over a hundred countries have laws like these.

Such laws work hand in hand with [[@free-speech|free speech]]. The right to say what you think matters more when you can check the facts first.

RTI requests have revealed missing ration grain, fake names on wage lists and delays in [[@pensions-old-age|pensions]]. Many people use it for small, personal problems, like finding out why a passport application is stuck, and the act of filing often gets things moving.

It has not been easy for everyone who uses it. Some RTI activists who exposed powerful people have been threatened or attacked, and campaigners have pushed for better protection. There are also arguments about whether recent changes to the law have weakened it. The [[@panchayat|panchayat]] office, the city council and the ministry in Delhi all have to answer the same kind of letter.

text: The United States has 50 states because it grew, step by step, [[@usa-statehood|from 13 colonies]] on the Atlantic coast to a country stretching across a continent and into the Pacific. Each time new land was settled and organised, it could ask to join as a state.

Each state has its own [[constitution|constitution]], governor, lawmakers and courts. Under the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]], powers not given to the national government belong to the states or the people. So states make many of their own rules, from driving ages to school calendars.

st.reveal: Alaska became the 49th state in January 1959, and Hawaii became the 50th that August. Texas joined back in 1845.

d.try: Find a map of the USA and look at the state borders. Mark the ones that are straight lines and the ones that follow rivers or coasts. Straight borders were often drawn by surveyors on paper, while wiggly ones usually follow nature.
myth: Washington, D.C. is in Washington state.
They are on opposite sides of the country, more than 3,500 km apart. Washington, D.C. is a federal district on the East Coast and is not part of any state. Washington state is in the far northwest.

sec.t:
In 1776, 13 British colonies [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|declared independence]] and fought the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]]. After winning, they at first worked together loosely, almost like separate countries. In 1787 they wrote a new Constitution to bind themselves into one nation. Delaware approved it first, on 7 December 1787, so it calls itself "the First State".

{{story:american-revolution}}

In 1803, the United States bought a huge area called Louisiana from France. The Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the size of the country. Later came Florida, [[@texas|Texas]], land in the west after a war with Mexico, and the Oregon Territory in the northwest. Settlers moved in, and new states were formed one after another.

This growth had a painful side. The land was already home to many Native American nations. Through wars, broken [[treaty|treaties]] and forced removals, most were pushed off their land as the states spread west.

A new state usually began as a [[territory|territory]] run by the national government. When enough people lived there, it wrote a constitution and asked [[@congress-usa|Congress]] to admit it. Arguments over [[@us-civil-war|slavery]] made this very tense in the 1800s, because each new state could tip the balance in the Senate.

[[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]] joined in 1912, completing the 48 states that touch one another. Then came two that do not touch the rest at all. [[@alaska|Alaska]], bought from Russia in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars, became a state in January 1959. [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]], a chain of Pacific islands once ruled by its own monarchs, followed in August 1959.

Every time a state joins, the flag gains a star. The 50-star flag came into use on 4 July 1960. Robert Heft, then a high school student in Ohio, said he designed it for a class project and first got a B minus. His design was later chosen, and his teacher changed the grade.

Alaska is the largest state, more than twice the size of Texas. Rhode Island is the smallest, smaller than many Indian districts. California has the most people, about 4 crore.

Because states make so many of their own laws, life can differ a lot across a border. The age for a driving licence, the sales tax on a toy, and even the date school starts can change when you cross from one state into the next. Each state also has its own nicknames and symbols. Texas calls itself the Lone Star State, and Hawaii is the Aloha State.

Some places are part of the United States but are not states. Washington, D.C. is a [[federal|federal]] district created to be the capital. [[@puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] and Guam are territories. People there are US citizens but do not have voting members in Congress. India took a different route, redrawing its map from inside rather than adding new land, as you can read in [[@states-india|Why is India divided into states?]].

text: Whole numbers are good for counting things that come in ones, like apples or children. But the world is full of parts. You might eat half a roti, wait a quarter of an hour, or share a [[@pizza|pizza]] among three friends. Fractions are how we describe and calculate with those parts.

A fraction has two numbers. The bottom one, the denominator, says how many equal pieces the whole is cut into. The top one, the numerator, says how many of those pieces you have. So 3/4 means three pieces of something cut into four. Without fractions, cooking, building, music, money and sharing would be much harder.

st.prompt: In the 1980s, the American chain A&W sold a third-pound burger, bigger than a rival's quarter-pounder, for the same price. Why did it sell badly?

options.t: Many people thought one third was smaller than one quarter
It tasted worse than the rival burger
It was too big to fit in the box

st.reveal: Customers saw the 3 in 1/3 and the 4 in 1/4 and assumed four was bigger. In fact, a third is more than a quarter. The company's owner, A. Alfred Taubman, later wrote about it in his memoir.

myth: A fraction with a bigger number on the bottom is bigger, so 1/8 is more than 1/4.

sec.h: A number on top of a number
sec.t:
Indian mathematicians, from at least the time of [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]] in the 600s, wrote fractions as one number above another, with no line between. Arab mathematicians adopted the idea and, by around the 1100s, added the bar between the two. Europeans learned it from them. The way you write fractions at school has a long journey behind it.

Fractions also live in everyday language. In [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] and many other Indian languages, there are single words for amounts like 1¼ (sawa), 1½ (dedh), 2½ (dhai) and ¾ (paune). Shopkeepers and grandparents use them without thinking. Some Indian children even learned "[[@multiplication-tables|times tables]]" for these, like the dhai ka pahada, the table of two and a half.

Music depends on fractions. In Western music, a whole note can be split into two half notes, four quarter notes or eight eighth notes. Musicians in the United States still use those names. Each [[@music-notes|music note]] tells a player how long to hold a sound, as a fraction of a beat.

Sport and time use them too. A football match has two halves. [[@basketball|Basketball]] games in the [[@nba|NBA]] have four quarters. "Quarter past nine" means 15 minutes, a quarter of an hour, after nine.

For centuries, Indian money was based on sixteenths. Sixteen annas made one rupee, and four paise made one anna. In 1957, India switched to a [[decimal|decimal]] system, with 100 naye paise in a rupee. The old word stays alive in phrases like "solah aane sach", sixteen annas true, meaning completely true.

American stock prices were quoted in fractions of a dollar, like 25 3/8, until about 2001, when markets switched to decimals. That habit went back to old Spanish silver dollars, which were often cut into eight pieces. Today, [[@decimals|decimals]] and [[@percentages|percentages]] are other ways of writing parts of a whole, and every one of them can be turned back into a fraction.

text: Madhava of Sangamagrama was a mathematician and [[astronomer|astronomer]] who lived in Kerala from about 1340 to about 1425. He founded what historians call the Kerala school, a chain of teachers and students that lasted about 200 years.

His big discovery was the infinite [[series|series]]: a sum with no last step, where each new piece is smaller than the one before. Madhava found series that give exact values for [[@pi|pi]] and for the sine and cosine used in measuring triangles. These ideas are central to calculus, the maths of change, which Europe developed in the 1600s.

st.prompt: Madhava's series for pi uses 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 and so on, forever. What happens if you stop after just a few terms?

options.t: You get a rough answer that slowly gets closer as you add terms
You get pi exactly after ten terms
The answer grows bigger and bigger without limit

st.reveal: The sum creeps towards pi ÷ 4, overshooting and undershooting by smaller amounts each time. It is very slow, so Madhava added a clever correction at the end to jump much closer.

src: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (Princeton University Press, 2009).
MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Madhava of Sangamagrama.
n.certNote: Madhava's exact dates and village are known only roughly, and almost none of his own writing on series survives. Historians agree the Kerala school's results came long before Europe's, but whether any of their ideas travelled to Europe is unproven.

myth: Calculus and infinite series were invented entirely in Europe by Newton and Leibniz.

Newton and Leibniz built calculus into a complete system in the late 1600s. But Madhava and his followers in Kerala had already found infinite series for pi, sine and cosine, ideas at the heart of calculus, about 250 years earlier.

sec.t:
Madhava lived in a village called Sangamagrama. Many historians think it was near Irinjalakuda, in today's Thrissur district of [[@kerala|Kerala]], though nobody knows for certain. He was a Brahmin astronomer whose main job was making accurate [[@calendars|calendars]] and predicting the positions of planets and [[@eclipses|eclipses]].

That practical work needed very exact values for pi and for sines. India had a long tradition of such calculation, stretching back to [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] in 499 CE. Madhava pushed it much further. His series for sine and cosine let astronomers calculate them to many [[decimal|decimal]] places without long tables. In Europe, Isaac Newton found the same series in the 1660s.

Almost none of Madhava's own writing about series survives. A few astronomy works with his name exist, but his mathematics reaches us through his students' students.

Around 1500, the astronomer Nilakantha Somayaji wrote the Tantrasangraha, which records Madhava's results. Soon after, Jyeshthadeva wrote the Yuktibhasha, in [[@malayalam|Malayalam]] rather than Sanskrit. It explains how the series were worked out, not just what they were, so it is sometimes called one of the earliest calculus textbooks. Many results were also written in verse, so students could memorise them.

In the 1500s and 1600s, Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries were active on the Kerala coast, and some studied local astronomy. A few historians suggest that Kerala's ideas could have travelled to Europe this way.

There is no clear evidence, such as a translated [[manuscript|manuscript]], that this happened. Most historians think Europe probably found the series on its own. Either way, the Kerala school reached these results first. [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] and Leibniz went on to build calculus into the general tool that physics and engineering now depend on.

For centuries, the outside world knew little of Madhava. In 1835, a British official named Charles Whish wrote a paper describing the Kerala series, but it was mostly ignored. Only in the 20th century did historians of mathematics, many of them Indian, study the manuscripts closely and give Madhava his due.

text: Star Wars, released in 1977, changed movies in several ways at once. Its special effects looked more real than anything audiences had seen. Its sound and music filled cinemas in a new way. And it earned so much money from tickets and toys that Hollywood studios began chasing giant "blockbuster" films with sequels and merchandise.

To make it, George Lucas had to start his own effects company, Industrial Light & Magic, which went on to work on hundreds of films. A small computer team at his company later became [[@pixar|Pixar]]. Much of how big films are made today traces back to that one space adventure.

st.prompt: In Star Wars, spaceships explode with huge bangs. What would you really hear if a ship exploded near you in space?

options.t: Nothing at all
A quieter bang, because space is big
A high-pitched whistle

st.reveal: Sound needs something to travel through, like air or water. Space is almost empty, so there is nothing to carry the sound. Film-makers add the bangs because silent explosions feel strange to audiences.

d.try: Be a sound designer. Find three everyday objects at home, like a metal spoon, a rubber band and a plastic bottle. Record the noises they make on a phone, then play them back while watching a short, silent cartoon clip, and pick which sound fits each moment best.
myth: You would hear explosions and laser blasts in space, just like in the films.
Space is nearly a vacuum, so sound cannot travel through it. A battle in space would be completely silent to anyone outside the ships.

sec.t:
In the mid-1970s, space films were out of fashion and many people thought Lucas's script was too strange. The studio gave him a modest budget. On its opening day in May 1977 it played in only a few dozen American cinemas.

Within weeks, queues stretched around the block. People watched it again and again. Star Wars became the highest-earning film released up to that time.

Lucas couldn't find anyone who could make the space battles he imagined, so in 1975 he set up Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) in California. Its team built detailed model spaceships, some only as long as your arm.

They also built a computer-controlled camera, called the Dykstraflex after its designer John Dykstra. It could repeat exactly the same move over and over. That let the team film each model separately and combine them, so dozens of ships seemed to zoom past together. ILM later created [[@special-effects|special effects]] for films from Jurassic Park to the Marvel series.

The sound designer Ben Burtt spent months collecting noises. The lightsaber hum mixed an old [[@projectors|film projector]]'s motor with buzz from a television set. The scream of a TIE fighter used an [[@elephants-talk|elephant's call]] blended with a car driving on a wet road. Chewbacca's roar mixed sounds from bears and other animals.

{{story:elephants-talk}}

In real space, none of these sounds could be heard. [[@sound-travel|Sound needs air]] or another material to travel through. Lucas added them anyway, because [[@space-weird-sound|a silent battle]] didn't feel exciting.

John Williams wrote a full orchestral score, at a time when many films used pop songs. His Star Wars theme is one of the most recognisable pieces of film music ever written.

Before the film came out, Lucas agreed to take a smaller fee as director. In return, he kept the rights to sequels and to merchandise like toys. Few people thought those rights were worth much.

They turned out to be worth a fortune. Star Wars action figures sold in huge numbers, and Lucas made more films. Studios learned that one hit could sell lunchboxes, games and books for decades. In 2012 Disney bought Lucasfilm for about US$4 billion.

Lucas borrowed from many places. He was inspired by old adventure serials, Westerns, and the Japanese director Akira Kurosawa's samurai films. He also read the writer Joseph Campbell, who studied hero myths from around the world.

That mix is part of why Star Wars travels so well. A farm boy who leaves home, a wise teacher, a princess who fights back and a villain in a black mask feel familiar to people everywhere. Many cultures have their own versions of these characters, which may be why the films feel like old stories even with spaceships in them.

sec.h: पानी कम पड़ने पर क्या होता है
sec.t:
शरीर इसे जल्दी भाँप लेता है। जैसे ही तुम अपने पानी का बस 1 या 2 प्रतिशत गँवाते हो, तुम्हें [[@thirst|प्यास]] लगती है। मुँह सूखने लगता है, और पेशाब का रंग गहरा हो जाता है, क्योंकि गुर्दे पानी बचाने लगते हैं। बहुत-से लोगों को सिरदर्द होता है और ध्यान लगाना मुश्किल लगता है।

लगभग 5 प्रतिशत पर लोग कमज़ोरी, चक्कर और उलझन महसूस करते हैं। लगभग 10 प्रतिशत से ज़्यादा हो, तो यह मेडिकल इमरजेंसी है। खून गाढ़ा हो जाता है और उसे पंप करना मुश्किल होता है, और [[organ|अंग]] काम करना बंद करने लगते हैं। डॉक्टर शरीर में पानी की गंभीर कमी का इलाज ड्रिप से तरल चढ़ाकर करते हैं।

अप्रैल 1979 में ऑस्ट्रिया में 18 साल के आंद्रेयास मिहावेत्स को एक कार दुर्घटना के बाद पुलिस की हवालात में रखा गया। गाड़ी में वे बस सवारी थे। तीन पुलिसवालों में से हर एक ने सोचा कि कोई और उनका ध्यान रख रहा है। वे 18 दिन तक भुला दिए गए।

वे बच गए, और गिनीज़ वर्ल्ड रिकॉर्ड्स उनके मामले को बिना खाने और पानी के ज़िंदा रहने का सबसे लंबा ज्ञात मामला मानता है। खबरों के मुताबिक उन्होंने दीवारों पर जमी ओस जैसी बूँदें चाटीं, यानी वे बूँदें जो ठंडी सतहों पर [[condensation|संघनन]] से बन जाती हैं। हो सकता है इनसे उन्हें बस ज़रूरत भर पानी मिल गया हो। यह मामला बहुत ही अनोखा है, और डॉक्टर कभी नहीं मानेंगे कि ज़्यादातर लोग इतने दिन टिक सकते हैं।

sec.h: मलबे के नीचे से बचे लोग
sec.t:
भूकंप के बाद बचाव दलों को कभी-कभी कई दिन बाद भी गिरी हुई इमारतों के नीचे लोग ज़िंदा मिलते हैं। वे अक्सर इसलिए बच जाते हैं क्योंकि वहाँ ठंडक होती है, वे ज़्यादा हिलते-डुलते नहीं, और हो सकता है उन्हें पाइपों या बारिश से थोड़ा-बहुत पानी मिल जाए।

ये किस्से दिखाते हैं कि ज़िंदा रहना हालात पर कितना निर्भर है। ठंडी, सीलन भरी जगह में चुपचाप बैठा इंसान धीरे-धीरे पानी गँवाता है। तपते रेगिस्तान में पैदल चलता इंसान पसीने में एक घंटे में एक लीटर से ज़्यादा गँवा सकता है।

कुछ जानवर सूखे हालात हमसे कहीं बेहतर झेल लेते हैं। [[@camels|ऊँट]] अपने शरीर का एक-चौथाई पानी गँवाकर भी सँभल जाते हैं, और लगभग 10 मिनट में करीब 100 लीटर पानी पी सकते हैं। उत्तरी अमेरिका के रेगिस्तानों का कंगारू चूहा शायद कभी पानी पीता ही नहीं, और अपने खाने से पानी पा लेता है।

भारत में थार रेगिस्तान का चिंकारा भी बिना पिए लंबे समय तक रह सकता है। वह पौधों और ओस से नमी पा लेता है।

गिलास गिनने की ज़रूरत नहीं। ज़्यादातर सेहतमंद बच्चों के लिए प्यास लगने पर, खाने के साथ और खेल-कूद के बाद पानी पीना काफ़ी है। तरबूज़, खीरा और दही जैसी पानी वाली चीज़ें भी मदद करती हैं।

बहुत गर्म दिनों में, खासकर [[@heatwaves|लू]] के समय, ज़्यादा पानी पियो और छाँव में आराम करो। और हाँ, तुम्हारे गिलास का पानी अरबों सालों से घूम रहा है, बादलों, नदियों और शायद एक-दो डायनासोरों से होकर भी, कभी न रुकने वाले [[@water-cycle|जल चक्र]] में।

text: खिलाड़ियों को भी वही सेहतमंद खाना चाहिए जो बाकी सबको, बस ज़्यादा मात्रा में और सही समय पर। दौड़ने, कूदने और बल्ला घुमाने का मुख्य ईंधन [[carbohydrate|कार्बोहाइड्रेट]] है, जो चावल, रोटी, मोटे अनाज, आलू, केले और दूसरे फलों में मिलता है। दाल, अंडे, दूध, पनीर, मछली, मांस और राजमा-छोले का [[protein|प्रोटीन]] ट्रेनिंग के बाद मांसपेशियों की मरम्मत करता है। सब्ज़ियाँ और फल [[vitamin|विटामिन]] और खनिज जोड़ते हैं। पानी सब कुछ चालू रखता है।

समय भी मायने रखता है। खेल से दो-तीन घंटे पहले ठीक से खाना, ज़रूरत हो तो हल्का नाश्ता, और खेल के बाद खाना और पानी, ये शरीर को उबरने में मदद करते हैं। कोई एक जादुई खाना नहीं है। सादा, तरह-तरह का खाना ही ज़्यादातर काम कर देता है।
नींद भी उतनी ही ज़रूरी है। मांसपेशियों की मरम्मत और ईंधन का भंडार दोबारा भरना ज़्यादातर आराम के समय ही होता है। इसलिए जो थका हुआ खिलाड़ी नींद छोड़ता है, वह कितना भी अच्छा खाए, पूरी तरह उबर नहीं पाता।

जब तुम कार्बोहाइड्रेट खाते हो, तो शरीर उसे तोड़कर ग्लूकोज़ नाम की शक्कर बना देता है। जो तुरंत काम नहीं आता, उसे वह ग्लाइकोजन के रूप में जमा कर लेता है। यह तुम्हारी [[@muscles|मांसपेशियों]] और लिवर में वैसे ही भरा रहता है जैसे गाड़ी की टंकी में पेट्रोल।

ज़ोरदार कसरत में मांसपेशियाँ ग्लाइकोजन तेज़ी से जलाती हैं। लगभग 90 मिनट तक ज़ोर से दौड़ने के बाद टंकी ख़ाली होने लग सकती है। मैराथन धावक इसे दीवार से टकराना कहते हैं: टाँगें सीसे जैसी भारी लगती हैं और हर कदम उठाना जंग लगता है। इसीलिए लंबी दूरी के धावक रेस से पहले के दिनों में खूब कार्बोहाइड्रेट खाते हैं, और दौड़ते हुए अक्सर छोटे-छोटे स्नैक या स्पोर्ट्स ड्रिंक लेते हैं।

ट्रेनिंग से मांसपेशियों के रेशों में बारीक-बारीक दरारें पड़ जाती हैं। प्रोटीन इनकी मरम्मत के लिए ईंटें देता है, और मांसपेशियाँ पहले से थोड़ी ज़्यादा मज़बूत होकर जुड़ती हैं।

युवा खिलाड़ियों को हर बार के खाने में थोड़ा प्रोटीन चाहिए, पर बहुत ज़्यादा नहीं। दाल-चावल की एक कटोरी, एक अंडा, एक गिलास दूध या एक कटोरी दही से यह जल्दी पूरा हो जाता है। भारत के बहुत-से शाकाहारी खिलाड़ी पनीर, सोया, अंकुरित अनाज और दालें खाते हैं। कुछ क्रिकेटर और पहलवान पारंपरिक खाने की कसम खाते हैं, और कुछ अब रागी जैसे [[@millets|मोटे अनाज]] भी जोड़ने लगे हैं, जिनसे हड्डियों के लिए कैल्शियम भी मिलता है।

युवा खिलाड़ियों के लिए दो खनिज बहुत अहम हैं। आयरन खून में ऑक्सीजन ढोता है, और इसकी कमी से थकान और साँस फूलने लगती है। यह हरी पत्तेदार सब्ज़ियों, राजमा-छोले, गुड़, अंडे और मांस से मिलता है। नींबू या आँवले जैसी विटामिन C वाली चीज़ें शरीर को इसे सोखने में मदद करती हैं। कैल्शियम हड्डियाँ बनाता है। हड्डियाँ अपना ज़्यादातर कैल्शियम बचपन और किशोर उम्र में ही जमा करती हैं। दूध, दही, रागी और तिल इसके अच्छे स्रोत हैं।

{{story:sports-science}}

शरीर पसीना बहाकर खुद को ठंडा करता है। चेन्नई या अमेरिका के फ़ीनिक्स की किसी गरम दोपहर में खिलाड़ी एक घंटे में एक लीटर या उससे ज़्यादा पसीना बहा सकता है। बहुत ज़्यादा पानी निकल जाए, तो थकान और चक्कर आने लगते हैं और सोचने की रफ़्तार धीमी पड़ जाती है।

इसका सीधा इलाज है कसरत से पहले, बीच में और बाद में [[@water-drink|पानी]] पीना, आख़िर में पूरी बोतल गटकने के बजाय छोटे-छोटे घूँट में। स्कूल के ज़्यादातर खेलों के लिए सादा पानी काफ़ी है। चीनी और नमक वाले स्पोर्ट्स ड्रिंक गरमी में लंबे, कड़े सेशन के लिए बने हैं। एनर्जी ड्रिंक की बात अलग है। उनमें कैफ़ीन होता है, और अमेरिकन एकेडमी ऑफ़ पीडियाट्रिक्स जैसे डॉक्टरों के संगठन कहते हैं कि बच्चों को ये नहीं पीने चाहिए।

बड़े खिलाड़ी पोषण विशेषज्ञों के साथ काम करते हैं, जो ठीक-ठीक नापते हैं कि उन्हें क्या चाहिए। [[@sports-science|खेल विज्ञान]] के वैज्ञानिक पसीने की जाँच करते हैं, ट्रेनिंग से पहले और बाद में खिलाड़ियों का वज़न लेते हैं, और मैचों के हिसाब से खाने की योजना बनाते हैं।

ज़्यादातर युवा खिलाड़ियों के लिए सलाह इससे आसान है। नियम से खाना खाओ, जिसमें अनाज, प्रोटीन वाली चीज़ें, फल और सब्ज़ियाँ सब हों। सुबह की प्रैक्टिस से पहले नाश्ता मत छोड़ो। खेल से पहले लंबा फ़ासला हो, तो केला, पोहा या मूँगफली की चिक्की जैसा कुछ खा लो। अगर वज़न, ताकत या खाने को लेकर चिंता हो, तो सप्लीमेंट आज़माने के बजाय माता-पिता, कोच या डॉक्टर से बात करो। किसी चैंपियन की थाली अक्सर घर की बनी एक अच्छी थाली जैसी ही दिखती है।

text: A memory card stores information as billions of tiny electrical charges, each one standing for a 0 or a 1. One 0 or 1 is called a bit. Eight bits make a byte, enough to store a single letter.

The cards in today's phones and [[@cameras-how|cameras]] hold anywhere from a few gigabytes to about 1 or 2 terabytes. A terabyte is roughly a million megabytes. That is enough for hundreds of thousands of photos, or a few hundred hours of video. The biggest cards can hold more than all the books in a large school library, turned into text, many times over.

st.prompt: About how many songs could a 1-terabyte memory card hold?

options.t: About 2,50,000 (a quarter of a million)
About 1,000
About 10 crore (100 million)

st.reveal: A typical song file is about 4 megabytes. A terabyte is about a million megabytes, so it holds roughly 2,50,000 songs. Played back to back, that is well over a year of music without a repeat.

myth: When you delete a file, it disappears from the card straight away.

Usually the device only marks that space as free, so it can be used again. The old data can stay there until something new is written on top. That is why special tools can sometimes rescue deleted photos.

sec.t:
Storage sizes climb in steps of about a thousand.

- A kilobyte (KB) is about a thousand bytes: a short [[@email|email]].
- A megabyte (MB) is about a million bytes: one song, or a phone photo.
- A gigabyte (GB) is about a billion bytes: a long film.
- A terabyte (TB) is about a trillion bytes.

To get a feel for those [[@big-numbers|big numbers]], think of each byte as a grain of rice. A gigabyte of rice would fill a small room. A terabyte would fill a large building.

{{story:big-numbers}}

sec.h: A disk the size of two fridges
sec.t:
In 1956, IBM sold a machine called the RAMAC 350. Inside was a stack of 50 spinning metal disks, each about 60 cm across. It weighed about a tonne and was roughly as big as two refrigerators. It could store about 3.75 megabytes, about the size of a single photo from your phone.

Companies rented it rather than buying it, because it was so expensive. Earlier computers stored data on punched paper cards, where each hole stood for a bit.

A memory card uses flash memory, invented by Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba in Japan in the 1980s. Inside are billions of microscopic cells built on a [[@chips-silicon|silicon chip]]. Each cell can trap a tiny bundle of electric charge, and keep it there even when the power is off.

A cell with charge might mean 0 and one without might mean 1. Newer cards squeeze in more by storing several levels of charge in each cell, so one cell can hold two, three or four bits. Nothing moves inside, which is why a memory card survives being dropped far better than the old spinning disks. Each cell does wear out slowly, though. After many thousands of rounds of being written and erased, it stops holding charge reliably, so the card quietly stops using it.

Your body has its own storage system, and it is far denser than any card. [[@dna|DNA]] stores the instructions for building you using four chemical letters instead of two. Scientists have managed to store books, pictures and even a short film in man-made DNA. One gram of DNA could in theory hold many millions of gigabytes. [[dna|DNA]] also lasts. Scientists have read DNA from [[mammoth|mammoth]] bones more than a million years old, while a memory card may lose its data after some years sitting unused in a drawer.

Reading and writing DNA is still slow and costly, so your photos are safe on silicon for now. But the idea that information can be packed into [[molecule|molecules]] is changing how engineers think about storage.

text: Emojis are designed in two stages. First, a group called the Unicode Consortium decides which emojis exist. It gives each one a code number and a short description, such as "face with tears of joy". Anyone can send in a proposal for a new emoji, but only a small number are accepted each year.

Then companies such as Apple, Google, Samsung and Microsoft hire artists to draw their own version of each one. That's why the same emoji can look slightly different on different phones. The code says what the emoji is. The company decides exactly how it looks.

st.prompt: You send a smiling emoji from an Android phone to a friend with an iPhone. What do they see?

options.t: The same emoji, but drawn in Apple's style
Exactly the same picture you saw
A blank box, because the phones can't talk

st.reveal: Your phone sends a code number, not a picture. Each company draws its own artwork for that number. So the meaning travels, but the exact face can look a little different on the other side.

Indian emoji added in 2019 include the diya lamp, the sari and the auto rickshaw

sec.t:
In the late 1990s, Japanese mobile phones could send short messages, but text alone could seem cold or unclear. In 1999, a designer named Shigetaka Kurita, working for the phone company NTT Docomo, drew a set of 176 small symbols: weather, hearts, faces, food and transport. Each was squeezed into a grid of just 12 by 12 [[@pixels|pixels]].

His set was not the very first. Another Japanese company had released a smaller set two years earlier. But Kurita's emojis became famous, and in 2016 the Museum of Modern Art in New York added them to its collection. The cute, simple style fits a wider love of cartoon images in [[@japan-culture|Japan]].

sec.h: How to get a new emoji
sec.t:
Anyone can write a proposal to Unicode. It must show that many people would use the emoji, that it can be recognised at a small size, and that it isn't already covered by another one. Proposals usually include sample drawings and evidence, such as how often people search for the word online.

A committee reviews them, and the process can take a year or two. Many ideas are turned down. Some that succeed come from ordinary people. A teenager in Saudi Arabia helped push for the hijab emoji, which arrived in 2017.

For years, emoji lists had little that felt Indian. That changed with the 2019 update, which added a diya lamp, a sari, an auto rickshaw and a Hindu temple. The Sikh khanda symbol was approved in 2022 and reached most phones in 2023. Emojis for many Indian festivals and foods are still missing, and people continue to send proposals.

Skin tone choices arrived in 2015. They let people pick from five shades for faces and hands, based on a scale doctors use to describe skin types.

Because companies draw their own versions, small differences can change the meaning. One "grimacing face" once looked like a nervous grin on one phone and an angry snarl on another. In 2016, Apple changed its pistol emoji into a green water gun, and other companies followed over the next few years.

Emoji designers work a bit like people who design [[@fonts|fonts]]. They must keep the meaning clear while giving each set a style of its own. It is strange to think that, like ancient [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]], small pictures have become part of how billions of people write every day.

text: A voice assistant, like the ones in smart speakers and phones, understands you in a few quick steps. First it listens for its wake word. Then it records what you say and usually sends the sound to powerful computers far away. Those computers turn the sound into text, work out what you want, and send back an answer, which the device speaks aloud.
All of this takes about a second or two. Each step uses a type of [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] trained on huge amounts of recorded speech and written text.

st.prompt: Before a smart speaker hears its wake word, where is it sending what it hears?

options.t: Nowhere. It checks short bits of sound on the device and throws them away
To the company's computers, every second of every day
Straight to your parents' phone

st.reveal: The device keeps a few seconds of sound in a tiny memory and checks it for the wake word. Only after it hears the word does it usually start sending your request to the company's computers. That is why its light changes when it wakes.

myth: Voice assistants understand language the way people do.

They match sound patterns to likely words, then match words to likely requests, using statistics learned from huge amounts of examples. They can be very good at this, but they don't share our experience of the world, which is why odd mistakes happen.

sec.t:
The device's [[@microphones|microphones]] are always listening, but a small chip inside only checks for one thing: the wake word, such as "Alexa" or "Hey Siri". It keeps a few seconds of sound in a short memory loop, checks it, and lets it vanish.

When the chip thinks it has heard the word, the device wakes up, its light changes, and it starts paying attention. Sometimes it gets it wrong and wakes up when someone on TV says something that sounds similar.

sec.h: Step two: from sound to words
Step three: working out what you mean
sec.t:
Turning sound into words is only half the job. "What's the weather like?" and "Will I need an umbrella?" use different words but mean almost the same thing. A second program, trained to understand language, sorts your request into a type, such as weather, music or timer, and picks out details like a place or a time.

Then the assistant does the job: it looks up the forecast, starts a song or sets the timer. Finally, a text-to-speech program turns the answer into a natural-sounding voice.

Early machines were very limited. Bell Labs' Audrey, in 1952, recognised spoken numbers. IBM's Shoebox, shown at the 1962 World's Fair in [[@seattle|Seattle]], understood 16 words, including the digits, and could do simple sums.

Real progress came when computers got fast enough to learn from huge recordings of speech. Apple added Siri to the iPhone in 2011. Amazon's Echo speaker arrived in 2014, and Google's Assistant in 2016.

Speech systems learn from the voices they are trained on. If those were mostly American voices, they may struggle with Scottish, Tamil or Texan accents. Indians often mix Hindi and English in one sentence, and companies have had to train special models to cope. With [[@languages-india|India's many languages]], there is still a long way to go.

Voice assistants are a big help for people who cannot see well or cannot use their hands easily. But they also raise questions about [[@privacy|privacy]]. Recordings are often stored, and in 2019 several companies admitted that human workers had listened to some clips to improve accuracy. Most now let users review and delete their recordings.

text: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was a teacher, writer and social reformer in nineteenth-century Bengal. He wrote a simple Bengali first reader, *Barnaparichay*, that children still learn from. He campaigned for widows to be allowed to remarry, and in 1856 a law made it legal.

He also fought child marriage, opened dozens of schools for girls and gave away much of his money to people in need. In Bengal he's remembered for his learning and his kindness alike, sometimes called *dayar sagar*, an ocean of kindness.

Light of Bengal

st.reveal: Vidya means learning or knowledge, and sagar means ocean or sea. His Sanskrit college gave him the title in 1839 for his outstanding scholarship.

sec.h: A poor boy who loved to read
sec.t:
Ishwar Chandra Bandyopadhyay was born in 1820 in Birsingha, a village in what is now West Bengal. His family was poor. When he was about eight, he walked with his father to Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], so he could study there.

A story often told says he learned English numerals on the way by reading milestones beside the road. Another says he studied at night under street lamps because his family couldn't afford oil. Whether every detail is exact, he became a brilliant student. In 1839 his Sanskrit college gave him the title Vidyasagar.

In 1855 he published *Barnaparichay*, meaning "introduction to letters". It taught the [[@bengali-language|Bengali]] alphabet in a clear order, with short words and simple sentences. He also tidied up the alphabet itself, settling on 12 vowels and 40 consonants for teaching.

The book was so clear that it is still used, more than 170 years later. Many Bengali speakers in India and Bangladesh learned to read from it.

He kept writing for young readers. *Kathamala* retold Aesop's fables in Bengali, and other books taught science, history and good habits in short, plain sentences. Before him, much written Bengali was stiff and full of long Sanskrit words. His clean style helped turn it into a language children could read for pleasure.

{{story:bengali-language}}

Vidyasagar became the head of Sanskrit College in Calcutta in 1851. At the time, only students from Brahmin families could study there. He changed the rules so students from other castes could join.

He believed girls deserved schooling too. He helped run the Bethune School, one of the first schools for girls in Calcutta, and in the late 1850s he helped set up about 35 girls' schools across Bengal. Around the same time, in Pune, [[@savitribai-phule|Savitribai Phule]] was teaching girls against fierce opposition.

In Bengal at that time, many girls were married very young. If their husbands died, even child widows were usually not allowed to remarry. They often lived hard, lonely lives.

Vidyasagar studied old Sanskrit texts and argued that they did not forbid widows from marrying again. He wrote books on the subject and gathered thousands of signatures on a petition. Many powerful people opposed him, and some threatened him. In July 1856 the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was passed. That December he helped arrange one of the first widow remarriages under the new law, and he later supported his own son's marriage to a widow.

Vidyasagar was famous for refusing to bow to people he thought were wrong, whether British officials or rich landlords. He was equally famous for generosity. When the poet Michael Madhusudan Dutt was in debt in France, Vidyasagar sent him money.

He continued earlier work by reformers such as [[@raja-ram-mohan-roy|Raja Ram Mohan Roy]], and he became a central figure of the [[@bengali-renaissance|Bengali Renaissance]], a time of new ideas in literature and society. He died in 1891. Today a university, colleges, a bridge over the Hooghly and countless schools carry his name.

text: The Rigveda, one of the oldest texts composed in India, praises a great river called Saraswati that flows from the mountains to the sea. One verse calls her the best of mothers, the best of rivers and the best of goddesses. Later texts say the river disappears into the desert. Today no river by that name reaches any sea.

Many researchers link it to the Ghaggar-Hakra, a river in Haryana, Rajasthan and Pakistan that flows mostly in the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. Its dry bed is in places several kilometres wide, much too wide for the trickle it carries now. So something big once flowed there. The arguments are about when, and what fed it.

st.prompt: Scientists think a big Himalayan river once flowed down the Ghaggar valley. Why did it stop, about 8,000 years ago?

options.t: The river, the Sutlej, slowly shifted its course to the west
An ancient king built a giant dam across it
An earthquake opened a crack that swallowed it

st.reveal: A 2017 study found that the Sutlej once ran down this valley and then wandered west. Rivers on flat plains do this, building up sand and silt until they spill into a new path.

sec.h: A river that vanished in the stories
sec.t:
In the Mahabharata, Balarama travels along the Saraswati on a long [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]]. The epic names a place called Vinashana, meaning "the vanishing", where the river sinks into the sand. That detail matters. Even 2,000 years ago, storytellers seem to have known a river that had shrunk.

Many Hindus today believe the Saraswati still flows unseen, underground. In this belief, it joins the Ganga and the Yamuna at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj, the meeting point where the [[@india-wonder-kumbh|Kumbh Mela]] gathers crowds bigger than most countries. For believers, the river is real whether or not a map shows it.

Here is the twist that made [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] sit up. Hundreds of settlements of the [[@indus-cities|Harappan civilisation]] lie along the Ghaggar-Hakra and its old branches. At Kalibangan in Rajasthan, diggers found a ploughed field about 4,800 years old, its furrows still visible in the soil. Rakhigarhi in Haryana, one of the biggest Harappan sites ever found, lies on the same plain.

People do not build towns in a waterless desert. So during Harappan times, roughly 4,600 to 3,900 years ago, this valley must have had water and good farmland.

A 2012 study led by Liviu Giosan suggested that, in Harappan times, the river was fed by [[monsoon|monsoon]] rain, not by Himalayan [[glacier|glaciers]]. In 2017, researchers from IIT Kanpur and Imperial College London found that the mighty Sutlej had once run down this valley, then shifted west about 8,000 years ago. The cities grew later, beside a gentler river that flooded less fiercely.

Other scientists argue that glacier water reached the valley for longer than that. Most agree that the monsoon weakened around 4,200 years ago and the river dried, around the time many Harappan towns emptied.

Matching a poem to a riverbed is tricky, because poets do not draw maps. Some historians are sure the Ghaggar-Hakra is the Saraswati of the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]]. Others say the hymns may describe a different river, or a memory blended from several. The Haryana government has even dug channels to bring water back along parts of the old course.

There is one more problem. The Rigveda was composed over centuries and passed down by memory long before anyone wrote it down, so nobody can pin its hymns to an exact year. Without a firm date, it is hard to say which version of the river the poets saw.

And rivers still wander. The Kosi in Bihar has shifted more than 100 kilometres west in about two centuries. It is a reminder that the rivers tumbling out of the [[@rivers-himalaya|Himalaya]] never promise to stay put.

text: In 1492, Christopher [[@columbus|Columbus]], sailing for Spain, reached islands in the Caribbean. Over the next 50 years, Spanish soldiers and settlers conquered huge parts of the Americas. They toppled the Aztec Empire in Mexico in 1521 and the Inca Empire in Peru in the 1530s.

The results were devastating for the people who already lived there. Diseases from Europe, especially smallpox, killed a very large share of the population. Survivors were forced to work in mines and on farms, and their religions and languages were pushed aside. At the same time, plants and animals crossed the ocean in both directions and changed what the whole world eats.

st.reveal: Smallpox, measles, influenza and other diseases spread faster than any army. People in the Americas had never met these germs, so their bodies had no defences. Wars and forced labour added to the deaths, but disease killed the most.

n.certNote: Historians agree that the Indigenous population of the Americas fell catastrophically after 1492, mostly from disease. How many people lived there before, and so how many died, is still debated, with estimates ranging very widely.

Steel weapons and horses helped, but the Spanish relied on tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, on rivalries inside the empires and, above all, on epidemics that had already killed many defenders.
