sec.t:
Columbus was looking for a sea route to Asia, which is why he called the people he met "Indians". The first lands he reached were islands such as Hispaniola, now Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The Taíno people who lived there were made to dig for gold and grow food for the newcomers.

Within a few decades, war, overwork and disease had almost wiped them out. A Spanish priest named Bartolomé de las Casas, who had once owned Indigenous labourers himself, became their fierce defender. He wrote angry reports to the Spanish king describing the cruelty he had seen. Spain passed laws to protect Indigenous people, but far from the king's eyes they were often ignored.

The Inca Empire stretched about 4,000 km along the Andes mountains. When Francisco Pizarro arrived in 1532, it had just been torn apart by a civil war between two royal brothers, and smallpox had already killed many people, including the previous emperor.

At the town of Cajamarca, Pizarro's small force ambushed the new emperor, Atahualpa, and captured him. Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold and two more with silver to win his freedom. The Spanish took the treasure and executed him anyway. Inca resistance continued for decades, but the [[empire|empire]] was broken.

Spain grew rich from the Americas. A single mountain at Potosí, in today's Bolivia, produced enormous amounts of silver, mined by Indigenous workers forced to labour there. Spanish silver coins spread so widely that they were used as money in China and in Indian ports.

As Indigenous populations collapsed, Spanish and Portuguese colonists turned to enslaved Africans to work on sugar plantations and in mines. Millions of people were carried across the Atlantic in chains, a history told in [[@slavery-freedom|slavery and freedom]].

Historians call the movement of plants, animals and germs between the [[hemisphere|hemispheres]] the Columbian Exchange. Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar cane went west to the Americas. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cocoa, peanuts and [[@chillies|chillies]] went east.

Portuguese traders brought chillies to India in the 1500s. Within a century they had become part of Indian cooking from Goa to Bengal. Today Mexico and Peru mix Spanish and Indigenous cultures. Millions of people still speak Indigenous languages such as Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, and Quechua, the language of the Inca.

text: Susan B. Anthony was an American campaigner who spent more than 50 years fighting for women's rights, especially the right to vote. She gave speeches across the country, wrote petitions, ran a newspaper and lobbied Congress year after year.

In 1872, she voted in a presidential election, which was illegal for women then, and was arrested. She died in 1906, before she could see women win the vote. But in 1920, the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution gave American women that right. It was nicknamed the "Susan B. Anthony Amendment" in her honour.

sec.t:
Anthony was born in 1820 in Massachusetts into a Quaker family. Quakers believed men and women were equal before God, and girls were expected to be educated. Her father, a cotton mill owner, was against slavery and alcohol.

She became a teacher and soon noticed that she was paid far less than male teachers for the same work. She began speaking out, first against slavery and against the harm caused by heavy drinking. When she wasn't allowed to speak at a temperance meeting because she was a woman, she started to focus on women's rights.

After the Civil War, the US Constitution was amended to protect the rights of formerly enslaved people. Anthony argued that these [[amendment|amendments]], which spoke of the rights of "citizens", already gave women the vote, since women were citizens.

On 5 November 1872, she and about 15 other women in Rochester, New York, cast ballots in the presidential election. Two weeks later, a marshal arrested her. At her trial in 1873, Judge Ward Hunt did not let her testify and ordered the jury to find her guilty. He fined her 100 dollars. She told him she would never pay, and she never did.

The fight for rights was not always united. After the Civil War, Congress proposed the 15th Amendment to give Black men the vote, but not women. Anthony and Stanton opposed it unless women were included. Others, including [[@frederick-douglass|Frederick Douglass]], who had long supported women's rights, believed Black men urgently needed the vote first.

The split was bitter, and some of Anthony and Stanton's arguments at the time used racist language. Historians today note this as part of her record. The two sides of the women's movement reunited in 1890.

Anthony kept travelling and speaking into her 80s. In 1906, at her last birthday celebration, she said "Failure is impossible". She died a month later.

Fourteen years after her death, in 1920, the 19th Amendment became part of the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]]. It says that the right to vote cannot be denied because of sex. Many Black women in the South, though, were still blocked from voting by unfair local rules until the 1960s.

In 1979, Anthony became the first real woman to appear on a regularly circulating US coin, the Susan B. Anthony dollar. Her house in Rochester is now a museum. On election days, voters in the city sometimes leave their "I Voted" stickers on her gravestone. In India, women won the right to vote with the first [[@constitution|constitution]] in 1950, on the same terms as men.

text: The Vedic age is the period after India's first great cities faded, roughly from 1500 to 500 BCE. It is named after the Vedas, four collections of hymns, chants and [[ritual|rituals]] in an early form of [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]].

At first, Vedic people were herders who moved with their animals across the land of rivers in the northwest. Cattle were wealth. Later, they settled in the plains of [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]], grew rice, used [[@iron-age|iron tools]] and formed small kingdoms. Much of what we know comes from the hymns themselves, which describe gods, battles, weddings, horses, rain and the daily wish for more cows.

st.reveal: Students learned the hymns by heart from teachers. They chanted each verse in several patterns, such as word by word, pairs of words and back again, so any mistake would stand out. UNESCO lists this chanting as part of the world's cultural heritage.

sec.t:
The Rigveda, the oldest Veda, has 1,028 hymns arranged in ten books. Nobody wrote them down for a very long time. Instead, boys trained for years with a teacher, chanting each verse again and again.

They learned it in clever patterns: word by word, then in pairs, then in pairs reversed. If anyone slipped, the pattern broke and the error showed at once. It worked like a checksum, the trick computers use to catch errors in data. This system kept the words steady for around 3,000 years, and UNESCO now lists Vedic chanting as part of humanity's cultural heritage.

sec.h: Gods of fire, storm and sky

sec.t:
Early Vedic life moved at the pace of a herd. Wars were often fought over cattle, and one word for battle meant "the search for cows". People drove light [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariots]] with spoked wheels, pulled by horses, and they raced them for sport.

Tribes met in assemblies called the *sabha* and the *samiti*, where leaders discussed matters together. A few hymns are said to be composed by women, such as Ghosha and Lopamudra, so some women clearly had a voice in religious life.

Over the centuries, Vedic people spread east into the forests and plains of the Ganga. Iron [[axis|axes]] and ploughs helped clear land. Villages grew into towns, and small tribes joined into kingdoms called *janapadas*.

Society changed too. People were sorted into groups called varnas, which slowly hardened into a strict order of birth. The later Vedic age also produced the Upanishads, thoughtful texts about the self and the universe. By about 500 BCE, new teachers such as the [[@buddha|Buddha]] were questioning old rituals.

The Vedas don't come with dates, and the Vedic people left few buildings. Historians piece the timeline together from the language, from iron tools found by [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] and from comparisons with related languages in Iran and Europe.

Sanskrit shares deep roots with Persian, Greek and Latin. Many scholars think its speakers came into India from Central Asia over many generations. Others argue the language grew up inside India. The debate continues, and new evidence from ancient DNA keeps adding fresh clues.

text: The Ganga begins at about 4,000 metres above sea level, where meltwater pours out of an ice cave at the end of the Gangotri Glacier. People call that cave Gaumukh, "the cow's mouth". From there the river runs about 2,525 km across northern India and Bangladesh to the Bay of Bengal.

Along the way it drops out of the mountains and crosses one of the flattest, most crowded plains on Earth. It picks up dozens of other rivers and finally splits into hundreds of channels in the Sundarbans. More than 40 crore people live in its basin, the land that drains into it.

The water comes from the Gangotri Glacier, about 18 km beyond the town, and from many other glaciers, streams and monsoon rains. Big tributaries such as the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak and Kosi add much more water along the way.

sec.h: Fast and cold in the mountains
sec.t:
Before it reaches Haridwar, about 290 km from the [[glacier|glacier]], the river falls more than 3,500 metres. The water is icy, grey with ground-up rock, and loud. This young stream is called the Bhagirathi, after a king in the Puranas who is said to have brought the river down from the heavens.

The Gangotri Glacier itself is about 30 km long, a river of ice that creeps downhill a few metres a year. Like most Himalayan glaciers, it is shrinking. The US Geological Survey reported that its snout moved back more than a kilometre between 1936 and 1996, and it has kept retreating since. Pilgrims who walk up to Gaumukh today stop farther upstream than their grandparents did.

At Devprayag the green Bhagirathi meets the muddier Alaknanda, and you can see the two colours side by side for a short stretch. From here on, the joined river is the Ganga. It runs through Rishikesh and leaves the hills at Haridwar, where much of its water is sent into canals to irrigate fields.

sec.h: Slow and wide across the plains

sec.t:
The Ganga river dolphin is India's national aquatic animal. It is almost blind and finds fish by sending out clicks and listening to the echoes. A 2025 survey counted about 6,300 river dolphins in the Ganga and nearby rivers. The river also holds gharials, a long-snouted crocodile that eats only fish, and freshwater turtles.

Pollution is a real problem. Sewage from cities and waste from factories flow in, and dams take water out. The government's Namami Gange programme, started in 2014, builds sewage plants along the banks. Scientists say some stretches are cleaner, while others still need a lot of work.

sec.h: Into the delta and the sea
sec.t:
At Farakka, in West Bengal, a barrage splits the flow. One branch, the Hooghly, runs south past [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]. The main river flows into Bangladesh, where it is called the Padma. There it meets the [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] and then the Meghna.

Together they build the Ganga Delta, the largest river [[delta|delta]] in the world. Its seaward edge is the Sundarbans, a maze of mangrove islands where tigers swim between the trees and the tide rises and falls twice a day. Every year these rivers carry about a billion tonnes of mud to the sea, so the coast keeps slowly changing shape. The ice that melted at Gaumukh months ago has finally become salt water.

text: Indian children have had their own magazines for over a century. In Bengal, *Sandesh* began in 1913. After independence came a wave of others: *Chandamama* in 1947, *Nandan* in Hindi in 1964, *Champak* in the late 1960s, *Balarama* in Malayalam in 1972 and *Tinkle* in 1980.

They were cheap, colourful and came in many languages. Most mixed folk tales, puzzles, jokes, science snippets, comics and readers' letters. For millions of families, the day a new issue arrived was a small festival, and older siblings fought younger ones over who read it first.

sec.t:
*Sandesh*, which means both "news" and a Bengali sweet, was started by Upendrakishore Ray Chowdhury, a writer, artist and printing expert. His son [[@sukumar-ray|Sukumar Ray]] filled it with nonsense rhymes and drawings that Bengali children still recite.

The magazine closed in the 1920s. In 1961, Sukumar's son, the film director Satyajit Ray, revived it with a friend. Ray wrote detective stories and science fiction for it, including his first tales of the sleuth Feluda. He also drew many of the covers himself.

In north India, *Nandan* and *Parag* carried stories, poems and quizzes in Hindi. *Champak*, from the Delhi publisher Delhi Press, was full of talking animals in a forest town. It now appears in several languages, including English. In Delhi, the cartoonist K. Shankar Pillai, known simply as Shankar, started the English monthly *Children's World* in 1968.

In Kerala, *Balarama* became one of the most widely read children's magazines in India. It mixed home-grown comics with translated ones. Tamil children had *Gokulam* as well as *Ambulimama*, the Tamil edition of Chandamama. Marathi children had *Kishor*. Many of these magazines also printed readers' drawings and letters, so a child in a small town could see their own name in print.

In 1980, Anant Pai, the man behind Amar Chitra Katha, started *Tinkle*. It brought India's best-loved comic characters: Suppandi, the servant who follows every order far too literally, and Shikari Shambu, the hunter who is terrified of animals and succeeds by luck. Readers sent in their own Suppandi stories, and the best ones were drawn and printed. Other regulars included Kalia the crow, who keeps rescuing smaller animals from a greedy jackal, and Tantri the Mantri, a minister whose plots to grab the throne always backfire.

In the USA, *Highlights for Children* has been posted to homes since 1946, with its hidden-picture puzzles. An older magazine, *St. Nicholas*, ran a club for young writers in the early 1900s. One of them, an eleven-year-old named Rachel Carson, later wrote *Silent Spring* and helped start the modern environmental movement.

Some Indian magazines closed when phones and television took children's time. *Nandan* stopped printing in 2020. Others now sell digital editions next to the paper ones. Grandparents still keep bundles of old *Chandamamas* tied with string, and grandchildren still find them.

text: A good story usually has a character the reader cares about, something that character wants badly, and a problem that gets in the way. The story follows what they do about it, and ends with something changed, either the situation or the character.

Beyond that, good stories tend to start quickly, show things happening instead of explaining them, and leave out the boring bits. Most of all, good stories are rewritten. Writers rarely get it right the first time, and the best ones keep fixing their stories until every sentence earns its place.

st.reveal: Readers keep turning pages to find out whether a character gets what they want. Without a want and an obstacle, even beautiful writing can feel flat. The trouble is what makes the story.

n.certNote: There is no single correct way to write a story. The tips here are ones many writers and teachers agree on, but plenty of great writers have broken every one of them.

myth: Good writers get it right the first time.
Almost all writers rewrite, cut and change their stories many times. First drafts are meant to be messy. The magic usually happens in the second, third or tenth draft.

sec.t:
Think of almost any story you love. Harry Potter wants to belong. Matilda wants to be treated fairly. In the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], a monkey wants to escape from a crocodile who plans to eat his heart. Wanting something gives a character a direction, and gives the reader a question: will they get it?

Then comes the obstacle. It can be a villain, a storm, a rule, a fear or another person who wants the opposite. The bigger and more personal the obstacle, the more readers worry, and worrying keeps them reading.

Many beginners start a story with the character waking up, brushing their teeth and eating breakfast. Readers get bored before anything happens. Experienced writers often start close to the trouble: a letter arrives, a dog runs away, a stranger knocks.

You can always explain the background later, a little at a time. A story is like a conversation with the reader. Nobody wants to hear a long list of facts before the interesting part.

The Russian writer Anton Chekhov gave advice that writers still repeat. In his letters, he said that if a gun hangs on the wall in the first act of a play, it should be fired by the last. In other words, don't include things that don't matter, and pay off the things you do include.

This works in reverse too. If your hero will need to climb a tree in the last chapter, it helps to show earlier that she is a good climber. Otherwise the ending feels like a cheat.

Roald Dahl wrote in a small hut in his garden in England, in pencil on yellow paper, and rewrote his pages again and again. Many writers say their first draft is just a way of finding out what the story is about.

When you finish a draft, put it away for a day. Then read it aloud. You will hear clumsy sentences and spot places where nothing happens. Cut them. Ask a friend which part they liked best and where they got bored. Then try again.

Nearly every writer says the same thing: read widely. Read [[@comics-art|comics]], poems, adventure books, myths and newspapers. Notice how other writers start stories, build suspense and end chapters. Keep a notebook for ideas, overheard words and strange things you see. One odd detail, like a cow standing on a bus stop at midnight, can be the seed of a whole story.

text: Kabir and Mirabai were two of the best-loved poets of the [[bhakti|Bhakti]] movement, a wave of devotion that spread across India between about the 7th and 17th centuries. Bhakti poets said that anyone could reach God through love, whatever their caste, religion or education.

Kabir was a weaver who lived in [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] in the 1400s. Mirabai was a princess from Rajasthan who lived in the early 1500s. They never met, and they were very different people. Both wrote in the everyday speech of ordinary people, not in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], and both are still sung today.

sec.h: Kabir, the weaver who asked hard questions

sec.t:
Kabir's best-known form is the doha, a [[couplet|couplet]] of two rhyming lines. Many Indian children learn this one at school: "I went searching for a bad person and found none. When I searched my own heart, I found no one worse than me."

His language mixed several north Indian [[@dialects|dialects]], the ancestor of modern [[@hindi-language|Hindi]]. A legend says that when he died at Maghar, Hindus wanted to cremate him and Muslims wanted to bury him. When they lifted the sheet, they found only flowers, and each group took half. It is a story about Kabir's message more than a record of what happened.

sec.h: Mirabai, the princess who chose Krishna
sec.t:
Mirabai was born into a [[@rajputs|Rajput]] royal family in Merta, in present-day Rajasthan. As a child, the story goes, she was given a small image of Krishna and decided he was her true husband.

She was married into the royal family of Mewar, whose capital was Chittor. After her husband died, she refused to behave as a royal widow was expected to. She sang and danced in temples with wandering holy people. Legends say her in-laws tried to poison her, and the poison turned to [[nectar|nectar]]. In later life she is said to have lived in Vrindavan and then [[@mystery-dwarka|Dwarka]], places linked with Krishna.

Mirabai's songs, called padas or [[@devotional-music|bhajans]], are about longing for Krishna, often as a beloved who is far away. They are full of everyday images: dark clouds, a dusty road, anklets ringing as she dances.

Hundreds of songs carry her name, though scholars think many were written later by others in her style. In 1945 the singer M. S. Subbulakshmi played Meera in a Tamil film and sang her songs, which carried them to new audiences across India.

Both poets spoke against the walls between people, Kabir with sharp humour and Mira with open-hearted song. Their verses turn up in classical concerts, folk music, [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] films and school textbooks. Kabir's followers formed the Kabir Panth, which still exists. When a song has been passed from voice to voice for five centuries, it has proved that [[@singing|singing]] can be as lasting as stone.

sec.t:
चॉकलेट की शुरुआत [[@chocolate-tree|कोको के पेड़]] की फलियों के अंदर के बीजों से होती है। यह पेड़ बस [[equator|भूमध्य रेखा]] के पास की एक गर्म, गीली पट्टी में उगता है। हर पाँच में से लगभग दो कोको बीज पश्चिमी अफ़्रीका के कोत दिव्वार से आते हैं। उसके बाद घाना है, और फिर इंडोनेशिया, इक्वाडोर, कैमरून और नाइजीरिया जैसे देश।

ज़्यादातर कोको लाखों छोटे किसान परिवार उगाते हैं, अक्सर ऐसे खेतों में जो कुछ क्रिकेट मैदानों से बड़े नहीं होते। बहुत-से परिवार बहुत कम कमाते हैं। कुछ इलाक़ों में बच्चे स्कूल जाने के बजाय कोको के खेतों पर काम करते हैं। चॉकलेट कंपनियाँ और सरकारें 20 साल से ज़्यादा समय से इसे ठीक करने का वादा कर रही हैं। [[@child-labour|बाल मज़दूरी]] के ख़िलाफ़ आवाज़ उठाने वाले समूह कहते हैं कि बदलाव धीमा रहा है।

[[@switzerland|स्विट्ज़रलैंड]] में कोको का एक भी पेड़ नहीं उगता। पर 1875 में वहाँ के चॉकलेट बनाने वाले डेनियल पीटर ने चॉकलेट में दूध मिलाने का तरीक़ा निकाला। इसके लिए उन्होंने अपने पड़ोसी हेनरी नेस्ले का बनाया दूध का पाउडर इस्तेमाल किया। कुछ साल बाद रुडोल्फ़ लिंट ने एक ऐसी मशीन बनाई जो चॉकलेट को कई दिनों तक चलाती रहती थी, जिससे वह मुलायम और मुँह में घुलने वाली बन गई।

स्विस चॉकलेट देश की शान बन गई और बड़े पैमाने पर [[export|निर्यात]] होने लगी। बेल्जियम भरावन वाली चॉकलेट, यानी प्रालीन, के लिए मशहूर है, और ब्रिटेन ने दुनिया को कैडबरी बार दी। हर देश का स्वाद थोड़ा अलग है। मेक्सिको में आज भी चॉकलेट अक्सर गर्म और झागदार पी जाती है, जिसे मोलिनियो नाम की लकड़ी की मथनी से फेंटा जाता है, बिल्कुल वैसे जैसे सदियों पहले। हमारे यहाँ छाछ बिलोने वाली मथानी याद आई न? अमेरिकी लोग अक्सर ज़्यादा मीठी चॉकलेट पसंद करते हैं, जबकि बहुत-से यूरोपीय लोगों को गहरी, डार्क चॉकलेट भाती है।

अमेरिका में चॉकलेट हैलोवीन, वैलेंटाइन डे और ईस्टर का हिस्सा है। वहाँ हर व्यक्ति साल में कई किलो चॉकलेट खाता है, और हर्शीज़ जैसी कंपनियाँ 1890 के दशक से चली आ रही हैं।

भारत में हर व्यक्ति इससे बहुत कम चॉकलेट खाता है, पर यह तेज़ी से बदल रहा है। बहुत-से भारतीयों ने पहली बार चॉकलेट कैडबरी की बार के रूप में ही चखी। इस कंपनी ने 1948 में भारत में चॉकलेट बेचना शुरू किया और बाद में यहाँ फ़ैक्टरियाँ भी खोलीं। आज दिवाली और रक्षाबंधन पर चॉकलेट का डिब्बा आम तोहफ़ा है। भारत थोड़ा कोको ख़ुद भी उगाता है, ज़्यादातर केरल, कर्नाटक और आंध्र प्रदेश में। अब कुछ छोटी भारतीय कंपनियाँ इन्हीं देसी बीजों से "बीन टू बार", यानी बीज से बार तक ख़ुद, चॉकलेट बनाती हैं।

2024 में पश्चिमी अफ़्रीका में ख़राब फ़सल की वजह से कोको के दाम रिकॉर्ड ऊँचाई पर पहुँच गए, और दुकानों में चॉकलेट या तो महँगी हो गई या छोटी। वैज्ञानिकों को चिंता है कि ज़्यादा गर्म और सूखा मौसम और पौधों की बीमारियाँ कोको उगाना और मुश्किल बना सकती हैं। कुछ किसान कोको को ऊँचे छायादार पेड़ों के बीच लगा रहे हैं, जो फ़सल और मिट्टी दोनों को बचा सकते हैं।

तुम तक पहुँचने से पहले हर बीज केले के पत्तों के नीचे ढेर में ख़मीर उठाता है, धूप में सूखता है, समंदर पार जाता है, भुनता है और पिसता है। यह लंबा रास्ता, जिसके बारे में [[@chocolate-making|चॉकलेट कैसे बनती है]] में पढ़ सकते हो, एक वजह है कि एक ही बार में घाना के बीज, ब्राज़ील की चीनी और आल्प्स पहाड़ों का दूध हो सकता है। चॉकलेट का एक छोटा टुकड़ा शायद उसे खाने वाले ज़्यादातर लोगों से ज़्यादा दुनिया घूम चुका होता है।

text: A food label is a small report about what is inside a packet. To read it well, look at three things. First, the ingredients list, which shows everything in the food, heaviest first. Second, the [[nutrition|nutrition]] table, which shows how much energy, fat, sugar, salt and [[protein|protein]] the food holds. Third, the small print: allergy warnings, the date and the vegetarian or non-vegetarian mark.

Indian labels usually give nutrition for every 100 g or 100 ml, and for one serving. American labels, called Nutrition Facts, give it per serving and add a "% Daily Value" to show how much of a day's need that serving covers. Once you know where to look, a packet can tell you a lot in under a minute.

sec.t:
Ingredients must be listed in order of weight at the time they went into the recipe. If sugar is the first or second ingredient in a [[@cereal-history|breakfast cereal]], that cereal is mostly sugar.

Companies sometimes split sugar into several different forms, such as sugar, glucose syrup and honey. Each appears lower down the list, even though together they might add up to the biggest ingredient. Reading the whole list, right to the end, gives the true picture.

India has a labelling rule that surprises many visitors. Every packet of food must carry a symbol. A green filled circle inside a green square means the food is vegetarian. A brown filled triangle inside a brown square means it contains meat, fish or egg. The non-veg mark used to be a brown circle. It was changed to a triangle, so the two marks now differ in shape as well as colour.

Families who are [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]], Jain or follow other food rules rely on these marks every day. Labels must also carry an FSSAI licence number, which shows the food maker is registered with India's food safety authority.

Allergy warnings matter a great deal for some people. Labels must name common [[allergen|allergens]], such as milk, nuts, wheat, [[@soybeans|soy]] or egg. Many add "may contain traces of nuts" if the food was made in a factory that also handles nuts. For someone with a serious [[@food-allergies|food allergy]], that line can matter more than anything else on the packet.

"Best before" means the food tastes and looks its best until that date, but may still be safe after it. "Use by" or "expiry" is about safety, and food should not be eaten after it.

In 1906, the American writer Upton Sinclair published *The Jungle*, a novel that described filthy conditions in Chicago's meat factories. Readers were horrified. The same year, the United States passed its first major food safety law. India's food laws were brought together under one act in 2006, which set up the FSSAI. Labels are one result of these rules: the right to know what you are eating.

text: The sandwich is named after John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, an English nobleman of the 1700s. The popular story is that he loved playing cards so much that he refused to stop for meals. Instead, he asked for meat tucked between two slices of bread, so he could eat with one hand and keep playing with the other. Others started asking for "the same as Sandwich", and the name stuck.

The Earl didn't invent eating things in bread. People had been doing that for thousands of years. But he made the idea fashionable among the rich in London, and the word spread from there around the world.

sec.h: The earl and the card table
sec.t:
The best-known account comes from a French writer named Pierre-Jean Grosley, who visited London in the 1760s. He described a government minister who spent 24 hours at a gambling table, eating only beef between slices of toast. He didn't name him, but readers took it to be the Earl of Sandwich.

The Earl was a busy politician. He was First Lord of the Admiralty, in charge of Britain's navy, for many years. His biographer, the historian N. A. M. Rodger, thinks the Earl was more likely eating at his desk while working late. Since the main source is one visitor's travel book, we will probably never know for sure.

sec.h: A town, a title and some islands

sec.t:
Long before the Earl, people wrapped food in bread. In ancient times, the Jewish teacher Hillel is said to have eaten lamb and bitter herbs between pieces of matzah, a flatbread, at Passover. Across the Middle East, people stuffed pita. In India, a roti rolled around sabzi or a kathi roll does the same job.

In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, thick slices of stale bread, called trenchers, served as plates. Diners ate the food on top, and sometimes the soggy bread too, or gave it to the poor.

Once the word spread, every country made the sandwich its own. In the USA, it became the peanut butter and jelly sandwich, the club sandwich and the burger. Is a [[@burgers-hotdogs|hot dog]] a sandwich? People still argue about that. Vietnam has the banh mi, Mexico the torta, Italy the panino.

In Mumbai, the "Bombay sandwich" is layered with green chutney, potato, cucumber, tomato and beetroot, often toasted on the street. The vada pav, a spicy potato fritter in a soft bun, is often said to have been first sold in 1966 by Ashok Vaidya near Dadar station. It became the fuel of Mumbai's mill workers, who needed cheap, fast food on the go. Today it's one of the city's best-loved [[@street-food|street foods]].

sec.h: A word that became a verb
sec.t: "Sandwich" has become more than food. We say a car was sandwiched between two buses, or that an ice cream sandwich holds ice cream between biscuits. Many other everyday words came from people's names, such as cardigan, from another British earl. Language is full of these accidental tributes, and the story of how English picks up new words is told in [[@words-borrowed|borrowed words]].

text: In much of South India, a full meal is served on a fresh green banana leaf instead of a plate. Rice sits at the centre, and around it come dal, sambar, rasam, vegetable dishes, chutneys, crunchy pappadams, [[@pickles-achar|pickle]], curd and a sweet like payasam. You [[@food-eating-with-hands|eat with your right hand]], mixing a little rice with each dish.

The leaf is waterproof, big, free in many places, and can simply be thrown away or fed to cows afterwards. At [[@festival-foods|weddings and festivals]], hundreds of guests sit in long rows, and servers walk down the line ladling dish after dish onto each leaf.

st.prompt: In a traditional Kerala sadya, which way does the narrow tip of the banana leaf point?

options.t: To the left of the person eating
Straight towards the person eating
Away from the person, towards the server

st.reveal: The leaf is usually laid with its narrow tip to the diner's left. Small side dishes go on the upper half, and rice is served on the wider lower half, close to the right hand.

sec.t:
Banana plants grow easily in the warm, wet south. Their leaves are large, tough and waxy, so they hold hot food and liquids without leaking. Hot rice slightly softens the leaf, which some people say adds a faint, fresh smell.

The leaf also solves the washing-up problem. After a feast for five hundred people, there are no plates to scrub. Used leaves break down quickly, and in villages they're often given to cattle. Compared with [[@pollution-plastic-land|plastic or paper plates]], they create almost no lasting rubbish, which is why some people point to them when talking about [[@recycling|recycling]] and waste.

The order matters. In a typical Tamil or Karnataka meal, rice comes first with a spoonful of ghee and a thick dal. Next comes sambar, a lentil stew with vegetables and [[@tamarind|tamarind]]. Then rasam, a thin, peppery, sour soup that many people drink straight from their palm.

Between these come vegetable dishes like poriyal or thoran, cooked with coconut. The meal ends with curd rice or [[@lassi-chaas|buttermilk]], which cools the mouth and stomach. A sweet may come in the middle or at the end.

In Tamil Nadu, the meal is called saapadu, and temple towns are famous for feasts served to pilgrims. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana are known for spicier meals, with fiery pickles, pappu (dal) and a sour green called gongura.

In Karnataka, an oota might include bisi bele bath, a hot rice and lentil dish. Udupi, a temple town on the Karnataka coast, gave its name to vegetarian restaurants across India, many of which serve "meals" on a steel plate lined with a banana leaf.

Most South Indians eat meals with their right hand. The fingers mix rice with sambar or rasam into small balls, and the thumb pushes each mouthful in. Many people say food tastes better this way, because you feel its warmth and texture before tasting it.

In cities, many people now eat from steel plates, and paper or areca-leaf plates are common at big events. But for festivals and weddings, the green [[@bananas|banana leaf]] still comes out.
